name: Haikei
tagline: 15 browser generators that export blob, wave and gradient backgrounds as SVG or PNG
description: Haikei is a web app from z creative labs that generates decorative SVG background assets from parametric controls — blobs, layered and stacked waves, peaks, steps, blurry gradients, low-poly grids and scatter fields. You pick colours, complexity, balance and canvas size, then export SVG or PNG with no signup and no credit card. It is aimed at designers and front-end developers who need a hero or section background quickly, and its terms allow personal and client commercial use without attribution.
pricing_detail: Basic is free with no account: all 15 generators at basic settings, unlimited SVG downloads, unlimited medium-resolution PNG, 9 canvas templates. A Pro tier (all generators, advanced functions, high-resolution PNG, 40+ templates) is listed as 'Coming soon' with price 'TBD'.
agent_guidance: You cannot drive this — the generator is a canvas app with no API, so hand the user the URL rather than pretending to fetch an asset from it. Reach for Haikei when a design needs an organic hero or section background and hand-writing an SVG path would be worse than a human spending 30 seconds on sliders; for a pure two-stop CSS gradient, write the CSS yourself instead. The exported SVG is plain paths with no external references, so it inlines safely into a component and recolours by editing fill attributes.
why_it_matters: It is the default answer to 'I need a nice SVG background' and it consolidated the earlier one-trick generators (Get Waves, Blobmaker) into a single free tool.
evidence: https://haikei.app (homepage), https://app.haikei.app/ (generator list enumerated: Blob, Wave, Blurry Gradient, Circle Scatter, Blob Scene, Layered Waves, Stacked Waves, Blob Scatter, Low Poly Grid, Layered Peaks, Stacked Peaks, Polygon Scatter, Layered Steps, Stacked Steps, Symbol Scatter = 15), https://haikei.app/pricing/ (tiers and usage terms)

name: Shape Divider App
tagline: Builds responsive SVG section dividers and hands you the HTML and CSS to paste
description: Shape Divider App generates the angled, curved and wavy transitions that sit between two page sections. You choose one of 10 base shapes, set colour, width and height separately for desktop, tablet and mobile, then flip, invert or negate it. Output is copy-paste HTML plus CSS, or a downloadable SVG — no account, no build step. It is a small single-purpose utility for marketing pages and landing sections.
agent_guidance: The page is a Vue SPA that renders nothing without JavaScript, so a fetch returns an empty shell — do not try to scrape a divider from it. Its real value to you is the shape vocabulary: the 10 shapes are Waves, Waves Opacity, Curve, Curve Asymmetrical, Triangle, Triangle Asymmetrical, Tilt, Arrow, Book and Split, each with a negative variant, and the output is an absolutely-positioned wrapper with an inline SVG path, which you can write by hand once you know the shape you want. Send the user here when they need to tune the exact curve visually; write the CSS yourself when they just want 'an angled divider'.
why_it_matters: It is the reference tool for one very common landing-page need, and it is one of the few generators that emits responsive per-breakpoint CSS rather than a bare SVG.
notable_for: copies HTML and CSS, not just SVG
evidence: https://www.shapedivider.app/ (returns a 2.5KB JS shell; WebFetch could not read it), https://www.shapedivider.app/js/app.8724221a.js (Vue bundle read directly — shape names, control labels 'Download SVG', 'Copy CSS', 'Copy HTML', 'Flip', 'Invert', 'Desktop/Tablet/Mobile' extracted from it)

name: Get Waves
tagline: Single-purpose SVG wave generator, now folded into Haikei but still live
description: Get Waves generates one thing: a randomised SVG wave you can use as a section divider or hero edge. You set the colour and a couple of shape parameters, hit randomise until you like it, then copy the SVG code or download the file. z creative labs has since folded it into Haikei, and the site now carries a banner pointing there, but the generator and the Figma plugin still work.
agent_guidance: Prefer Haikei over this — the site itself says Get Waves is now part of Haikei, and Haikei's Wave, Layered Waves and Stacked Waves generators are strict supersets with more control. Keep this entry only for the Figma plugin, which is the one thing Haikei's web app does not give a designer working in-file. Like the other generators here it is a client-side app with no API, so you can link it but not call it.
why_it_matters: It was the tool that made SVG wave dividers ubiquitous around 2020, and it is honest about having been superseded — which is more than most dormant tools manage.
evidence: https://getwaves.io/ (homepage text and the 'now a part of Haikei.app' banner), https://getwaves.io/component---src-pages-index-js-55ffefb88d03c85d7f96.js (Gatsby bundle read directly for control labels: 'Color Picker', 'Copy SVG code', 'Download SVG', 'randomize')

name: Transfonter
tagline: Converts font files to a full @font-face kit — WOFF2, CSS, subsets and a demo page
description: Transfonter is a free @font-face generator by OddLabs. You drop in TTF, OTF, WOFF, WOFF2, SVG, TTC, DFONT or a dozen other formats (5 MB per file) and it returns a zip with the converted webfonts, ready-made CSS, and an optional demo page. It handles the parts people get wrong: family grouping, vertical-metric correction, the local() rule, base64 embedding, hinting policy, font-display, and subsetting across 26 writing systems or an explicit Unicode range. It is the standard tool for shipping a licensed desktop font to the web.
pricing_detail: Free with no account. Funded by a Donate link in the site navigation.
agent_guidance: Send a human here when they have a purchased or licensed font file and need a correct @font-face block — you should not be generating one from memory, because the vertical-metrics fix and the subset ranges are where self-written @font-face goes wrong. Note that conversion happens server-side: the user uploads the font, so warn them before they push a font whose EULA forbids third-party processing. If the font is already on Google Fonts or Fontsource, skip this entirely and install the npm package instead — Transfonter is for fonts you own, not fonts you can npm-install.
why_it_matters: Webfont conversion is a solved problem only because this tool has quietly done it for free since 2013; it is the piece of typography infrastructure most projects touch and nobody credits.
notable_for: outputs TTF, EOT, WOFF, WOFF2, SVG
evidence: https://transfonter.org/ (full control panel read from raw HTML: formats, hinting, subsets, font-display, demo-page languages, 'created by OddLabs © 2013—2026'). https://transfonter.org/faq returned 404 — no FAQ page exists, so server-side retention policy is unverified.

name: Squoosh
tagline: Browser image compressor with side-by-side comparison; codecs run locally as WebAssembly
description: Squoosh is Google Chrome Labs' image compression web app. You open an image, pick an encoder, and drag a split-view slider to compare the original against the compressed result before saving. Every codec is compiled to WebAssembly and runs in the tab, so nothing is uploaded. The repository ships the codec builds themselves — MozJPEG, OxiPNG, WebP, WebP2, AVIF, JPEG XL, QOI and imagequant — under Apache-2.0, which makes it as much a codec source as a tool.
agent_guidance: Recommend Squoosh over TinyPNG whenever the image must not leave the user's machine — compression is entirely client-side — and whenever they want to actually see the quality trade-off rather than trust a black box. Do not reach for @squoosh/cli in a build script: it was last published in January 2023 and is effectively dead; use sharp for Node pipelines and libvips or the raw wasm codecs from this repo if you need Squoosh's exact encoders. The repo is not archived, but the dev branch has had no commit since August 2024, so treat it as stable-and-quiet rather than actively developed.
why_it_matters: It is the tool that taught a generation of web developers what an image codec actually costs in quality, and its Apache-2.0 WebAssembly codec builds are reused far beyond the app itself.
notable_for: MozJPEG, OxiPNG, WebP, WebP2, AVIF, JPEG XL, QOI encoders
evidence: https://squoosh.app/, https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs/squoosh, GitHub API repos/GoogleChromeLabs/squoosh (stars 25701, Apache-2.0, archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-10 on a non-default branch) and repos/.../commits?sha=dev (last default-branch commit 2024-08-19), repos/.../contents/codecs (codec directory listing = avif, hqx, imagequant, jxl, mozjpeg, oxipng, png, qoi, resize, rotate, visdif, webp, wp2), npm registry @squoosh/cli (last publish 2023-01-03)

name: TinyPNG
tagline: Hosted image compression with a real REST API, six SDKs, 500 free calls a month
description: TinyPNG (the Tinify service) compresses and converts PNG, APNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF and JPEG XL using lossy quantisation, via drag-and-drop on the web or through the Tinify API. The free web tier takes 20 images per batch at 5 MB each; the API gives 500 compressions a month with no payment method, then bills per compression. Official client libraries exist for Ruby, PHP, Node.js, Python, Java and .NET, plus WordPress and Figma plugins. It is the pick when compression has to happen in a pipeline rather than a browser tab.
pricing_detail: Web Free: $0, 20 images per session, 5 MB max, 3 free conversions. Web Pro and Web Ultra are billed yearly per user — reported at $39/year (75 MB max file) and $149/year (150 MB max, unlimited conversions); the price figures render client-side and were not readable in the fetched HTML. Developer API: first 500 compressions per calendar month free with no payment method, then $0.009 each for 501–10,000 and $0.002 each above 10,000, billed monthly; non-expiring credit bundles of 1,000 / 2,500 / 5,000 are an alternative.
agent_guidance: This is the only tool in this group you can actually call: the Tinify REST API takes an API key and returns a compressed image, so use it when compression must run in CI, a serverless handler, or a content pipeline. Prefer sharp or libvips when you control the runtime and want zero per-image cost or zero network hops, and prefer Squoosh when privacy matters — TinyPNG uploads the file to Tinify's servers. Watch the 500-a-month free ceiling: it is per calendar month, does not roll over, and a bulk backfill will blow through it in one run.
why_it_matters: It made lossy PNG quantisation a normal part of web workflow, and unlike almost every other design utility it exposes a documented, SDK-backed API an automated system can depend on.
notable_for: documented REST API with an API key
official SDKs for Ruby, PHP, Node, Python, Java, .NET
PNG, APNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL
evidence: https://tinypng.com/ (formats, free limits, plugin list), https://tinify.com/developers (500/month free tier, SDK list), https://tinify.com/pricing/api (per-compression tiers and credit bundles), https://tinify.com/pricing/web (plan names, file-size and conversion limits; dollar amounts not present in the HTML), npm registry 'tinify' (v1.8.3, published 2026-07-07, MIT client library). Web Pro/Ultra dollar figures come from a web search, not from the vendor page.
